::: {.why}
The last piece of week 11, and the reason a failure to reject a unit root is even weaker evidence than yesterday's power curve suggested.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Show that a stationary series with one mean shift fails to reject the unit root null, and say why the test cannot tell the two apart.
- Say what you would do about a suspected break when you have no prior about its date.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Construct the counterexample: simulate a stationary AR(1) with coefficient 0.5 and a single mean shift halfway through the sample, then run ADF. It will fail to reject. Repeat 500 times and report the rejection rate as a function of the size of the shift.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Look for it in real data: run ruptures on the 10-year yield and on a credit spread over twenty years, and compare the detected break dates against ADF results on the full sample and on each detected segment separately. A series that is a unit root over the whole sample and stationary within every segment is the standard finding.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the rule you will follow into your notebook: what you do when the break date is known in advance, and what you do when it is not, which is a different and much weaker position to be in.
:::
:::
